blocks.content: Think about how you actually download a movie torrent versus how you stream something on a service backed by one company's servers.
With streaming, your request goes to their server, their server does all the work, and sends the data back to you. If that server is slow or down, you get nothing.

With a torrent, you are pulling pieces of the file from a dozen different strangers' computers at the same time, and your own computer is also handing pieces to other strangers downloading the same file. Nobody is "the" server. Everybody is a little bit of everything.

Peer-to-peer architecture is a design where every node in the network can act as both a client and a server, sharing resources directly with other nodes instead of routing everything through one central machine.

["Client-server
One machine (or a farm of them) does the serving. Everyone else just consumes.","Peer-to-peer
Every machine consumes and contributes. There is no single machine the whole system depends on."]
items:
Client-server
One machine (or a farm of them) does the serving. Everyone else just consumes.

Peer-to-peer
Every machine consumes and contributes. There is no single machine the whole system depends on.

blocks.content: That one shift, from "one server for everyone" to "everyone serves a little," changes how these systems scale, how they fail, and how hard they are to reason about. That is what this topic is about.
1. Introduction
In a normal client-server setup, clients ask, servers answer. The roles never swap. Your browser never serves a webpage back to Google.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396524937-712695994.png
blocks.alt: A central server pushing data out to three separate clients

blocks.content: P2P architecture throws that split away. Every participant, usually called a peer or a node, can request data from other peers and also serve data to them. There is no dedicated machine sitting at the center that everything depends on.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525600-472062249.png
blocks.alt: Four peers connected directly to each other with no central server

blocks.content: This is not a niche idea. File sharing networks, blockchain networks, and some early chat and calling apps are all built this way, and the reasons come down to how P2P handles growth and failure differently from client-server.

blocks.title: Not fully decentralized
blocks.content: Most real P2P systems still lean on a little bit of centralization somewhere, like a bootstrap server or a tracker, just to help peers find each other. Pure, zero-central-anything P2P is rarer than people assume, and you will see why in section 4.
2. Why P2P scales differently

Client-server scaling is a spending problem. More users means more load on the same server, so you buy bigger servers or add more of them behind a load balancer, and you keep paying for that capacity whether or not it is fully used.
2.1 Every peer contributes and consumes
In P2P, a new peer joining the network is not pure extra load. It also brings its own upload bandwidth, storage, and CPU to the table.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525602-629465036.png
blocks.alt: A new peer pulling data from one peer while sharing data with another

blocks.content: Picture a torrent swarm with a thousand people downloading the same file. Each of those thousand machines is also uploading pieces it already has to other people in the swarm. The more people join, the more total upload capacity exists across the swarm, which is the opposite of how a single file server behaves under the same load.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525602-625132498.png
blocks.alt: One peer node acting as both a server role and a client role at the same time

blocks.content: That is the core trick. A peer is not just a mouth to feed, it is also a pair of hands. This is why P2P networks can serve huge numbers of users a wildly popular file without any single machine getting crushed.
2.2 Client-server vs P2P at a glance
blocks.text: 2.2 Client-server vs P2P at a glance

blocks.content: Neither model is strictly better. They just make different tradeoffs, and picking the right one depends on the workload.

{"headers":["Client-Server","Peer-to-Peer"],"rows":[["One place to look for data, easy to reason about","Data is spread across many peers, harder to pin down"],["Server is a single point of failure","No single peer leaving takes the whole system down"],["Scaling costs money, you provision more servers","Scaling is partly free, peers bring their own resources"],["Easy to enforce rules, permissions, and consistency","Hard to enforce anything without a central authority"],["Great for workloads needing strong consistency","Great for bulk content distribution and resilience"]]}
Most real products actually blend both, which is exactly what section 4 is about.
3. How peers find each other
Here is the part that trips people up first. If there is no central server, how does a brand new peer even know any other peer exists?
3.1 Bootstrap nodes
The simplest answer is a bootstrap node, sometimes just called a seed node. It is a well known, always-on address that new peers connect to first, purely to get introduced to the rest of the network.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525603-110070838.png
blocks.alt: A new peer asking a bootstrap node for a list of existing peers

blocks.content: Once the new peer gets back a handful of addresses from the bootstrap node, it connects to those peers directly, and from then on it can learn about even more peers just by talking to the ones it already knows. The bootstrap node's job is done after that first introduction.

blocks.title: A bootstrap node is not the whole network
blocks.content: It does not route data, it does not store the actual content, it just answers "who else is out there." Bitcoin, BitTorrent, and most P2P chat apps all use some flavor of this to get a new node its first few connections.
3.2 Distributed hash tables

Bootstrap nodes solve "how do I find any peer." A distributed hash table, or DHT, solves a harder problem: "how do I find the specific peer that has the exact piece of data I want," without any single machine holding an index of everything.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525603-976563129.png
blocks.alt: A lookup hopping across three peers to reach the one holding the key

blocks.content: At a conceptual level, a DHT like Kademlia gives every peer an ID, and every piece of data a key, both from the same numeric space. To find data, you do not ask a central index, you ask a peer that is "closer" to that key than you are, and that peer forwards you to a peer even closer, and so on. Each hop narrows the search, similar to how you would not search a phonebook page by page, you would jump to roughly the right letter first and then narrow down.

blocks.title: You will not be asked to implement Kademlia
blocks.content: For interviews, knowing that DHTs let peers find data without a central index, and that they route lookups by "distance" between IDs, is enough depth. Save the exact XOR metric details for when you actually need to build one.
4. Pure P2P vs hybrid P2P
In practice, "P2P" is a spectrum, not a single design. It helps to separate two flavors.
4.1 Pure P2P

In a pure P2P network, every function, discovery, lookup, and the actual data transfer, happens between peers with zero dedicated central infrastructure. Early Gnutella worked close to this way, flooding queries from peer to peer to find who had a file.

["Upside
Nothing to shut down or block. No company or server owns the network.","Downside
Discovery is inefficient, since queries have to spread peer to peer instead of hitting one fast index."]
items:
Upside
Nothing to shut down or block. No company or server owns the network.

Downside
Discovery is inefficient, since queries have to spread peer to peer instead of hitting one fast index.

blocks.content: 4.2 Hybrid P2P
Most systems people actually use are hybrid. A small centralized piece helps peers find each other, but the heavy lifting, the actual file transfer, stays strictly peer to peer.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525603-228634818.png
blocks.alt: A tracker handing out peer lists while peers exchange the actual file data

blocks.content: BitTorrent is the textbook example. A tracker, or a DHT acting like one, tells your client which peers in the swarm have the file you want. Your client then downloads the actual bytes directly from those peers, never from the tracker itself. The tracker only ever handled introductions.

blocks.title: Why hybrid wins in practice
blocks.content: A little centralization makes discovery fast and reliable, while keeping the expensive part, moving actual data, spread across everyone. You get most of P2P's scaling benefit without pure P2P's discovery pain.
5. Where P2P shows up in the real world
blocks.text: 5. Where P2P shows up in the real world

blocks.content: P2P is not just a torrenting trick. It shows up anywhere a system needs to distribute either bulk data or trust across many independent machines.
5.1 BitTorrent

Still the clearest example. A popular file gets downloaded by thousands of people, and instead of one server sweating under that load, every downloader also becomes an uploader for pieces they already have.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525604-691990786.png
blocks.alt: Your client pulling different pieces of a file from three separate peers

blocks.content: The busier the swarm, the faster downloads tend to get for everyone, since there are simply more sources for every piece of the file.
5.2 Blockchain networks

Bitcoin and most other blockchains run on P2P networking under the hood. When you broadcast a transaction, it does not go to one central server, it gets relayed peer to peer, node to node, until the whole network has seen it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525605-124215124.png
blocks.alt: A transaction relaying from node to node across a small network

blocks.content: New blocks propagate the exact same way. This is core to why blockchains do not have one company that can just be switched off to stop the network. There is no headquarters to raid.
5.3 Early P2P chat and VoIP

Before everything moved to centralized cloud backends, some chat and voice call apps, early Skype being the famous case, routed calls and messages directly between users' machines when possible, only falling back to relay servers when direct connections were not possible, usually because of firewalls or NAT.
Most of that has since moved back toward centralized or hybrid backends for reasons this topic covers next, but it is a good reminder that P2P is not limited to file sharing.
6. Worked example: downloading a file with BitTorrent
blocks.text: 6. Worked example: downloading a file with BitTorrent

blocks.content: Say you want to download a five gigabyte Linux distro image, and two hundred other people are downloading the exact same file right now.

blocks.title: Same file, two hundred sources
blocks.text: Your BitTorrent client reads a small .torrent file, which lists a tracker address and a hash for every piece the full file is broken into, usually a few hundred pieces of a few hundred kilobytes each. It contacts the tracker, gets back a list of peers currently in the swarm, and starts connecting to as many of them as it can. Instead of asking one server for the whole file in order, it asks different peers for different pieces, often the rarest pieces first so no single piece becomes a bottleneck later. As pieces arrive, your client verifies each one against its hash, then immediately starts offering that piece to other peers who do not have it yet. By the time your download finishes, you have probably uploaded a meaningful chunk of data back into the swarm too.

blocks.content: Compare that to downloading the same file from a single company server. One server, no matter how beefy, has a hard ceiling on total upload bandwidth. Two hundred simultaneous downloaders sharing pieces among themselves do not hit that same ceiling, because the "server" here is effectively two hundred machines' worth of upload bandwidth combined.
7. The real challenges of P2P
None of this comes for free. P2P trades away some of the guarantees client-server gives you almost automatically.
7.1 Peers are unreliable

A server you pay for stays up because someone is paid to keep it up. A random peer is just someone's laptop, and it can close the app, lose its connection, or shut down at any second, with zero warning to anyone relying on it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525605-921253389.png
blocks.alt: One peer disconnecting mid transfer while another peer takes over

blocks.content: Good P2P systems are built assuming peers will vanish constantly, a behavior called churn. That means always having more than one source for the same data, and being ready to reroute to a different peer the instant one drops.

blocks.title: Design for churn from day one
blocks.content: If your protocol assumes peers stay connected, it will fall apart the first time real users close their laptop lids. Redundancy is not optional in P2P, it is the whole safety net.
7.2 No central authority
There is no admin account, no one machine that can say "this data is correct" or "this peer is banned." That is a feature for censorship resistance, and a genuine headache for everything else.

["Trust
Nothing stops a malicious peer from sending you corrupted or fake data, so systems need their own checks, like BitTorrent verifying every piece against a hash.","Rule enforcement
There is no server to ban a bad actor outright. Blockchains handle this with consensus rules baked into every node instead of one enforcer.","Moderation
Anything requiring a judgment call, like taking down content, has no single throat to choke."]
items:
Trust
Nothing stops a malicious peer from sending you corrupted or fake data, so systems need their own checks, like BitTorrent verifying every piece against a hash.

Rule enforcement
There is no server to ban a bad actor outright. Blockchains handle this with consensus rules baked into every node instead of one enforcer.

Moderation
Anything requiring a judgment call, like taking down content, has no single throat to choke.

blocks.content: 7.3 Consistency and discovery are hard

When data lives on one server, you always know exactly where to look and you get one consistent answer. When data is scattered across thousands of unreliable peers, "where is this specific piece of data right now" and "is this the latest version" both become genuinely hard questions.

blocks.title: This is why DHTs exist
blocks.content: A distributed hash table is essentially an answer to the discovery half of this problem, giving you a way to route a lookup to the right peer without a central index. It does not solve consistency though, that is a separate, still-hard problem in most P2P designs.
8. A protocol sketch

You will not build a full P2P stack in an interview, but sketching the shape of the protocol shows you understand what is actually happening under the hood. Here is a stripped down version of the handshake a peer runs through in a swarm-style protocol.

Two things worth noticing here. First, joining and downloading are separate steps, discovery through the bootstrap node happens once, transfer happens continuously after. Second, every incoming piece gets verified against its hash before being trusted or shared further, which is the whole answer to "how do you trust data from a random stranger's machine."
9. The interview angle
P2P rarely carries a whole system design interview on its own, but it comes up as a strong answer in two specific situations.

["Bulk content distribution
If someone asks how to distribute a huge file, patch, or update to millions of machines without melting your servers, mentioning a P2P or BitTorrent-style distribution layer is a legitimate, real-world answer, plenty of software updaters actually do this.","Blockchain or decentralized systems
If the question involves anything decentralized, no single owner, censorship resistance, trustless networks, P2P networking is the transport layer underneath almost all of it."]
items:
Bulk content distribution
If someone asks how to distribute a huge file, patch, or update to millions of machines without melting your servers, mentioning a P2P or BitTorrent-style distribution layer is a legitimate, real-world answer, plenty of software updaters actually do this.

Blockchain or decentralized systems
If the question involves anything decentralized, no single owner, censorship resistance, trustless networks, P2P networking is the transport layer underneath almost all of it.

blocks.content: You do not need to reimplement Kademlia on a whiteboard. You need to recognize when a workload wants peers sharing load with each other instead of one server carrying everyone, and be able to explain why.
10. Quick recap
P2P architecture turns every node into both a consumer and a provider of resources, which is the opposite of the fixed client-server split.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396525605-705696851.png
blocks.alt: A server outage affecting every client compared to one peer outage affecting nobody else

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Scales with more peers instead of against them","Peers are unreliable and can disappear anytime"],["No single point of failure","No central authority to enforce rules or trust"],["Cheaper at scale, peers bring their own resources","Harder to guarantee consistency or find data fast"],["Resistant to being shut down or censored","Debugging and reasoning about the system is harder"]]}

Bootstrap nodes get a new peer its first connections, DHTs help peers find specific data without a central index, and most systems you will actually encounter are hybrid, a small centralized piece for discovery, pure P2P for the actual data transfer. That combination is why BitTorrent and blockchains both hold up at massive scale without one server anywhere near the middle of it.
